chunks.text:
Condition or topic: Ocular allergy, specifically allergic conjunctivitis (seasonal and perennial)

Clinical background: Ocular allergy represents a set of often underappreciated immune-mediated inflammatory conditions affecting the anterior eye surface, encompassing various clinical presentations in both children and adults. Allergic conjunctivitis is the most common form and is sub-classified into seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and perennial allergic conjunctivitis depending on whether the triggering aeroallergen is seasonal or present year-round; grass pollen is the most frequent sensitizer in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, whereas dust mites and animal dander predominate in perennial allergic conjunctivitis. The prevalence of ocular allergy has been rising globally for decades, with seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis affecting between 14% and up to 45% of the general population depending on geographic area. Despite this, allergic conjunctivitis remains underdiagnosed and undertreated—only 10% of affected individuals seek medical attention, with most self-managing using over-the-counter products and non-pharmacological remedies. Ocular allergy frequently coexists with other ocular disorders such as infections and dry eye disease, markedly impairs quality of life, and imposes a substantial economic burden. Management encompasses preventive, non-pharmacological, and pharmacological strategies. First-line pharmacotherapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and agents with dual activity, while corticosteroids and immunomodulators are reserved for severe keratoconjunctivitis. Because many patients receive topical treatments for prolonged periods, the short- and long-term safety and ocular surface tolerability of these preparations are critical; certain excipients in ophthalmic solutions can disrupt the epithelial barrier and tear film, potentially leading to dry eye or exacerbation of allergic conjunctivitis. The review aims to collate current evidence on these therapeutic options.

chunks.text:
Main findings:
  - Description: Emedastine was found to be superior to levocabastine in terms of efficacy.
    Context: Reference [27]
  - Description: Olopatadine demonstrated superiority over emedastine.
    Context: References [29, 30]
  - Description: Olopatadine showed similar symptom reduction to some dual-action agents.
    Context: Reference [28]
  - Description: Cetirizine ophthalmic solution significantly reduced ocular itching and conjunctival redness compared to its vehicle.
    Context: Clinical trial NCT01881113; references [32–34]
  - Description: Bilastine ophthalmic solution demonstrated a fast onset of action and maintained efficacy for up to 16 hours post-administration, supporting once-daily dosing.
    Context: References [31, 38]
  - Description: In a phase III trial, bilastine showed similar efficacy to ketotifen 0.025% multi-dose formulation.
    Context: References [35, 39]
  - Description: Olopatadine, ketotifen, alcaftadine, and bepotastine exhibit a similar efficacy profile, though some studies indicate bepotastine and alcaftadine may be superior to olopatadine.
    Context: References [43–45]
  - Description: Ketotifen 0.025% was effective in managing seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, but patient-reported outcomes favored olopatadine 0.1% solution for comfort and efficacy.
    Context: Reference [46]
  - Description: In terms of clinical relief and tolerability, dual-action agents were superior to antihistamines like levocabastine and mast cell stabilizers such as lodoxamide or cromolyn.
    Context: References [7, 28]
  - Description: Intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone furoate, mometasone furoate) significantly improved ocular allergic symptoms compared to placebo.
    Context: References [7, 52]

chunks.text:
Safety results:
  Notable adverse events:
    - Bilastine: uncommon adverse reactions; common side effects include increased ocular discomfort, eye burning/stinging upon instillation, dry eye, blurry vision, eye discharge, eye irritation, lacrimation.
    - Cetirizine: common side effects include hyperaemia, lid oedema, keratitis, eye pain.
    - Emedastine: common adverse events include itchy eyes, eye pain, redness of the eyes, burning sensation, watery eyes.
    - Levocabastine: common adverse events include blurred vision, eye irritation, pain, swelling, itching, redness.
    - Alcaftadine: taste perversion and bad taste, eye irritation, burning and/or stinging upon instillation.
    - Azelastine: common side effects include punctate erosion of corneal epithelium, eye pain.
    - Bepotastine besilate: common side effects include abnormal sensation in eyes, burning sensation, eye irritation, punctate keratitis.
    - Epinastine: common side effects include eye irritation, dry eye.
    - Ketotifen: common side effects include eye irritation, eye pain, eye pruritus, eye redness.
    - Olopatadine: common side effects include eye irritation, eye pain, mild transient irritation.

chunks.text:
Secondary results:
  - Preservative-free formulation of bilastine co-formulated with hyaluronic acid preserved tear film and ocular surface integrity in preclinical studies.
  - Patient preference: olopatadine 0.1% was preferred over ketotifen 0.025% in a study measuring comfort and efficacy.
  - Bilastine phase III trial showed non-inferiority compared to ketotifen 0.05%.
  - Cetirizine ophthalmic solution demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and was well tolerated.
  - In a pediatric study, ketotifen was safe and effective in children aged 7–15 years.
  - Preservative-free single-dose and multi-dose formulations of ketotifen, olopatadine, and azelastine are available in some European countries.

chunks.text:
Interpretation: After reviewing current evidence, the authors interpret that allergic conjunctivitis is frequently underdiagnosed and may benefit from a multidisciplinary approach. Management involves a stepwise strategy: allergen avoidance based on allergy testing, first-line pharmacological treatment with topical antihistamines or dual-action agents, with preference for preservative-free formulations and hyaluronic acid co-formulation to protect the ocular surface and improve compliance.

Clinical implications:
  - Allergic conjunctivitis is prevalent and often underdiagnosed, and a multidisciplinary approach can aid diagnosis in patients with compatible symptoms and common concomitant conditions.
  - Preservatives in ophthalmic solutions induce ocular surface damage, exacerbate seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis, and may lead to dry eye disease.
  - Co-formulation with hyaluronic acid has potential benefits including improved ocular surface wound healing, prevention of dryness, and increased ocular bioavailability of active drugs.
  - Dosing frequency influences treatment compliance: simpler dosing regimens correlate with higher adherence.

Practice implications:
  - Perform an allergy study as part of management to guide allergen avoidance measures.
  - Use topical ophthalmic antihistamines or dual-action drugs as first-line pharmacological treatment for allergic conjunctivitis.
  - Prefer preservative-free ophthalmic solutions to avoid ocular surface damage.
  - Consider formulations with hyaluronic acid to protect the ocular surface and potentially enhance drug bioavailability.
  - Favor once-daily dosing when possible to improve patient adherence.
  - Choose single-dose or preservative-free multi-dose devices for anti-allergic topical treatments.
  - A recently developed once-daily, preservative-free, antihistamine formulation with hyaluronic acid is now available as a treatment option.

chunks.text:
Main conclusion: The management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis should prioritize topical therapies that effectively control signs and symptoms while minimizing iatrogenic damage to the ocular surface, as many commercial formulations contain preservatives like benzalkonium chloride that can disrupt the tear film and exacerbate dry eye disease.

Narrative summary: This review updates the topical management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC), the most common forms of ocular allergy, emphasizing the importance of tear film integrity and the potential harm from ophthalmic solution additives. SAC and PAC are IgE-mediated, often underdiagnosed, and frequently comorbid with allergic rhinitis and dry eye disease. First-line pharmacological therapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and dual-action agents, with recent additions like bilastine 0.6 mg/ml (preservative-free, once daily, co-formulated with hyaluronic acid) and cetirizine 2.4 mg/ml. However, many older products contain benzalkonium chloride (BAK), a preservative that disrupts the epithelial barrier and may promote dry eye. The review tabulates approved multi-dose formulations, detailing their excipients, dosing, and preservative content. For instance, levocabastine, emedastine, and several dual-action agents contain BAK at varying concentrations, while preservative-free single-dose options exist for ketotifen, olopatadine, and azelastine. Topical vasoconstrictors and NSAIDs are discouraged due to limited efficacy and adverse effects, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases under ophthalmological supervision. Allergen immunotherapy remains an option when avoidance and pharmacotherapy fail. In summary, clinicians should select topical agents not only for their antiallergic efficacy but also for their formulation’s impact on the ocular surface, preferentially using preservative-free or low-toxicity preparations to optimize long-term safety and tolerability.
